opus-5.5.text:
Looking back, I think vid2vid was an early attempt at the same core question we're asking now with world models: can a neural network learn to generate the visual world in a way that's consistent over time? In 2018, when we did vid2vid, the setup was conditional. We gave the model a semantic segmentation map, edge maps, or pose sequences, and asked it to render photorealistic video frame by frame. The key challenge then was temporal coherence. If you generate each frame independently, things flicker. So we used optical flow, warped the previous frames, and let the network fill in what was new. That idea, that the past constrains the future and the model has to learn what persists and what changes, is very much at the heart of world modeling.

The difference is the scale and the ambition. Back then we were working with GANs, relatively small datasets like Cityscapes, and fairly short clips at modest resolution. The model was a renderer more than a simulator. It didn't really understand physics or cause and effect. It was translating one representation into another. Today, with diffusion models, transformers, and training on enormous amounts of video, we can ask the model to predict how the world evolves given actions or text, not just to paint pixels over a layout. That's a shift from "rendering" to "simulating."

There's also a lineage in between. After vid2vid we did few-shot vid2vid, then world-consistent vid2vid, where we tried to keep the generated world consistent in 3D as the camera moved, and GANcraft, and work like GameGAN, which learned to imitate a game engine from gameplay. Each of those pushed toward the model holding a persistent internal state of the world. Those were small steps, but they shaped how I think about the problem.

So I'd say vid2vid was a seed. It convinced me that neural networks could be graphics engines, and that video generation is not just about making nice content. It's a path to building simulators for physical AI, for robots and autonomous vehicles, that can learn from data rather than being hand-crafted. The world-model work we're doing now is that same intuition, just with far better tools and a much clearer sense of why it matters.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, I think vid2vid was really an early, narrow form of what we now call a world model. Back in 2018, the question we were asking was: given some structured description of a scene — a semantic segmentation map, a pose skeleton, an edge map — can a network synthesize a photorealistic video that is temporally consistent? That was the hard part. Image-to-image translation worked frame by frame, but the moment you stacked frames together you got flickering, objects popping in and out, textures swimming around. So a lot of the engineering in vid2vid was about conditioning on previous frames, using optical flow to warp the past into the present, and designing discriminators that looked at the temporal dimension, not just the spatial one.

In hindsight, what we were actually learning was a conditional distribution over how the visual world evolves. The model had to implicitly understand that a car in frame t moves smoothly to frame t+1, that lighting on a building doesn't change randomly, that occlusions resolve in physically plausible ways. That is world-modeling, just in a very constrained setting where we handed the model the layout and asked it only to render.

The big differences with today's work are scale and the control signal. First, we were training on a few thousand video clips of driving or faces; now we train on hundreds of millions of hours. The architecture also changed — GANs gave us sharpness but were painful to train and hard to scale, and diffusion and autoregressive transformers gave us something far more stable that just keeps improving with compute. Second, and more importantly, the conditioning moved from "here is the exact layout, please paint it" to "here is a text prompt, or a robot action, or a camera trajectory — you figure out what happens next." That shift means the model now has to carry the physics and the semantics itself, instead of borrowing them from an input segmentation map. That's what makes it a world model rather than a neural renderer.

But I'd say the motivation is continuous. The reason I cared about vid2vid was never really about making pretty videos. It was that if you can synthesize realistic, controllable video, you have a simulator, and simulators are how you train agents without the cost and danger of the real world. That's exactly the framing we take with Cosmos today — world foundation models as the data engine and the training ground for robots and autonomous vehicles. So I see vid2vid as one of the first steps on that path. We had the right goal, we just didn't have the data, the compute, or the right generative framework yet to make the model general.

astra-6.text:
I see vid2vid as an early step toward one part of what people now call a world model: generating a visually coherent world over time. The connection is temporal consistency. It’s not enough to make one frame look convincing; what you generate next has to make sense relative to what came before.

But I would distinguish video synthesis from modeling how the world works. In vid2vid, the generation is guided by an input sequence, so much of the structure of what happens is supplied to the model. A world model has a broader ambition: to predict how a scene evolves, potentially in response to an action.

So there’s a continuity in the visual-generation problem, but also an important shift—from rendering a supplied sequence to learning the dynamics that produce the sequence. Making a video look plausible is part of that challenge; making its behavior reliable is another.

sol-6.1.text:
I see a connection in the goal of generating a temporally consistent visual world, but I would be careful about equating video generation with a world model. With vid2vid, the problem is more like: given a sequence describing what should happen, can we turn that into realistic video while maintaining consistency over time? Much of the structure is already supplied to the model.

For a world model, the ambition goes further: can the model predict how the world changes, especially in response to an action? The distinction is between rendering a specified sequence and learning the dynamics that produce that sequence. A video can look convincing without having the right causal behavior.

So I would view vid2vid as an early piece of that broader direction. Visual synthesis is valuable, but the key question for a world model is whether its predictions remain useful when you act on them.
